title: Beyond Endozoochory: New World Oropendolas Also Disperse Large Seeds via Stomatochory
content: Identifying seed dispersal mechanisms is key to understanding plant responses to global change and, ultimately, ecosystem resilience. New World Oropendolas (Icteridae) are widespread frugivorous birds traditionally regarded as seed dispersers through endozoochory, acting as gulpers swallowing whole fruits and as mashers when biting into large fruits with pulp, and later defecating viable seeds. Here, we provide photographic evidence that Crested Oropendolas (Psarocolius decumanus) also disperse whole fruits through stomatochory by transporting them in their bills. We observed individuals removing fruits from oil palms (Elaeis guineensis), carrying them in flight, and subsequently consuming the pulp while holding the fruit against branches with their feet. Previously, we also observed Montezuma Oropendolas (Psarocolius montezuma) carrying fruits of three plant species in flight. In all cases, the plants produced large fruits and seeds whose dispersal by endozoochory would be constrained by their size. These observations reveal a previously overlooked dispersal mechanism in a widespread group of Neotropical frugivores and suggest that the role of oropendolas in seed dispersal may be broader than previously recognized.
